Watch and ReadTheodore Roosevelt

Unit 2.2, The Progressive Era

Theodore Roosevelt was born in New York City in 1858, into a great deal of money and a body that did not work. Asthma nearly killed him more than once before he was ten. He rebuilt himself deliberately, first in a gymnasium his father built on the second floor of the house, then on a cattle ranch in the Dakota Badlands, and the rebuilt version is the one the country met.

By forty he was a war hero. At forty two he was the youngest president the United States had ever had. He broke up corporations, sided with striking miners against their owners, and put more land under federal protection than every president before him combined. He also took the Canal Zone from Colombia, declared the United States the police force of Latin America, won a Nobel Peace Prize, and spent most of his adult life looking for a fight.

The eight portraits below are all the same person. Work through them first, then watch the two clips. The clips do not agree with each other, and neither does he.

Roosevelt Over the Years

Click a face. Every one of these is the same man.

The Sickly Child 1869

He wanted to be able to breathe.

Asthma kept him sitting upright through entire nights while his father drove him around New York in a carriage looking for air that would move. The family could buy him anything except a working set of lungs.

When he was twelve his father told him he had the mind but not the body, and that he would have to make the body. A gymnasium went in on the second floor. He started lifting and never really stopped. What he took from it was a conviction that weakness is a decision. He would eventually apply that rule to entire nations.

The Harvard Athlete 1878

He wanted to be counted among strong men, and he wanted his father to see it.

He boxed at Harvard, took real beatings in the ring, and lost the lightweight final. The photograph is a young man showing you a body he built on purpose.

His father died during his sophomore year. Roosevelt called him the best man he ever knew and spent the rest of his life measuring himself against him. From this point on he proved things in public, with his body, in front of a crowd.

The Assemblyman 1884

He wanted to break the arrangement between corporate money and Albany politics, and he wanted a name before he turned thirty.

He got both faster than anyone expected. He was in the New York Assembly at twenty three and running investigations into corruption within a year.

Then on February 14, 1884, his wife Alice and his mother died in the same house on the same day. He drew a cross in his diary and wrote that the light had gone out of his life. He did not say Alice's name in public again. Grief is the reason for the next photograph.

The Dakota Rancher 1885

He wanted to disappear into open country and rebuild himself somewhere nobody had heard of him.

He bought cattle in the Badlands and worked them himself. He chased a gang of boat thieves down the Little Missouri in early spring and sat reading Tolstoy while he guarded them.

The blizzards of 1886 and 1887 killed most of his herd and a large share of his fortune. He came back east with something he valued more than the money: a character. The eastern gentleman who could ride. He wore it for the rest of his career and the country believed every bit of it.

The Navy Man 1897

He wanted a war, and he wanted a fleet that could win one.

As Assistant Secretary of the Navy he was second in command of the department and behaved as though he were first. He pushed for battleships, told audiences the country had gone soft on easy living, and wrote to friends that almost any war would do. In October 1897 he used his influence to put Commodore George Dewey in command of the Asiatic Squadron, because he wanted a man out there who would act without being told twice.

On the afternoon of February 25, 1898, Secretary Long left him in charge of the department. Roosevelt cabled Dewey to gather the squadron at Hong Kong, keep full of coal, and in the event of war begin offensive operations in the Philippines. Nobody reversed the order. Two months later Dewey destroyed the Spanish fleet at Manila Bay and the United States had an empire in the Pacific.

The Rough Rider 1898

He wanted to be in the fighting himself, in a place where people could watch him do it.

He resigned the desk job and raised a volunteer cavalry regiment out of cowboys, Ivy League athletes, and lawmen. On July 1, 1898, he led it up Kettle Hill outside Santiago, mounted, ahead of his men. He called it the great day of his life.

He was famous within weeks and governor of New York within months. The lesson the charge taught him, and taught the country watching him, was that war had worked.

Governor and Vice President 1899 to 1901

He wanted to run New York on his own terms. What he got instead was a job designed to keep him quiet.

He was elected governor three months after Cuba. He taxed corporations that were used to being left alone and refused to take orders from the party machine, and he made himself such a problem that Senator Thomas Platt worked to get him nominated for vice president in 1900 mainly to move him out of the state.

The vice presidency had almost no duties at all. He held it for six months and was bored senseless. Mark Hanna is supposed to have asked his fellow Republicans whether they understood that there was now only one life between that cowboy and the presidency.

The President 1901

He wanted the presidency to be the strongest thing in American government, and then he used it that way.

On September 14, 1901, McKinley died of an assassin's bullet and Roosevelt took the oath in Buffalo, the youngest man ever to hold the office.

In seven years he broke up trusts, forced mine owners to settle with striking coal miners, set aside roughly two hundred and thirty million acres of public land, took the Panama Canal Zone, announced that the United States would police Latin America, and won the Nobel Peace Prize for ending somebody else's war. He also discharged an entire battalion of Black soldiers without trial after Brownsville. That is one man, in one presidency, and this page is not going to sort him out for you.

Timeline

  1. 1858 Born in New York A wealthy family on East 20th Street, and a child who cannot reliably breathe.
  2. 1878 His father dies Roosevelt is a sophomore at Harvard and calls him the best man he ever knew.
  3. 1884 Two deaths in one house His wife and his mother die on the same day. He walks away from politics.
  4. 1884 He goes to the Badlands Two years running cattle in the Dakota Territory.
  5. 1886 He comes home broke Blizzards kill the herd. He returns east with a reputation instead of a fortune.
  6. 1895 Police Commissioner He walks New York beats at night to catch officers asleep on duty.
  7. 1897 Assistant Secretary of the Navy He builds up the fleet and argues in public for a war with Spain.
  8. 1898 Kettle Hill He resigns, raises the Rough Riders, and becomes a national hero in one summer.
  9. 1899 Governor of New York He taxes corporations and infuriates the bosses who put him there.
  10. 1900 Vice President Senator Platt engineers the nomination mainly to get him out of the state.
  11. 1901 President at 42 Parked in the vice presidency, then McKinley is shot in Buffalo.
  12. 1901 Dinner at the White House He invites Booker T. Washington to dine. White newspapers across the South erupt.
  13. 1902 He sides with the strikers The coal strike ends with a president backing labor against the owners.
  14. 1903 Panama He supports the revolt against Colombia and the United States takes the Canal Zone.
  15. 1904 The Roosevelt Corollary Europe stays out of Latin America and the United States polices it instead.
  16. 1906 Brownsville and the Nobel He discharges Black soldiers without trial, and wins the Peace Prize the same year.
  17. 1908 He hands the party to Taft He had promised in 1904 not to run again, and he keeps the promise.
  18. 1910 He breaks with Taft At Osawatomie he calls for a New Nationalism, and starts attacking his own successor.
  19. 1912 He loses the nomination He challenges Taft, wins most of the primaries, and loses the convention anyway.
  20. 1912 Bull Moose He runs third party. In Milwaukee a man shoots him in the chest and he finishes the speech.
  21. 1912 Wilson wins Roosevelt beats Taft and splits the party. The Democrats take the White House.
  22. 1915 He turns on Wilson He attacks neutrality as cowardice and campaigns for the country to arm and fight.
  23. 1917 Wilson refuses him He asks to raise a volunteer division for France. The president says no.
  24. 1918 Quentin His youngest son is shot down over France. Roosevelt never really recovers.
  25. 1919 He dies at 60 In his sleep, at home, still angry about the war he was not allowed to join.
